title: Only comfort
hook: the Heidelberg Catechism begins: what is your only comfort in life and death?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luther's barber: four strands through one commandment. Your line was a simple way to pray.

What is your only comfort in life and in death? That's the very first question of a catechism, a book of questions and answers for teaching the faith. It doesn't open with the nature of God or the order of the universe. It opens with the question someone asks at a sickbed, or lying awake in the small hours. The book is the Heidelberg Catechism, named for the German city it came from, and still taught in some Reformed churches. Some learn its first answer by heart and carry it for life.

Here's the answer, put plainly. That I am not my own. That I belong, body and soul, in life and in death, to my faithful Savior Jesus Christ. It goes on: he has paid for my sins and set me free; he watches over me so that not a hair can fall from my head without the Father's will; and by his Spirit he makes me willing and ready to live for him. Comfort here isn't a mood that comes and goes. It's a fact about belonging: whose you are. It starts with a negative, not my own, close to Paul's words: "ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price." To some ears that sounds like a loss. The catechism hears it as relief. If I am not my own, I don't have to hold myself together. Someone faithful is holding me. And to the Romans: "whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord's." The hairs of your head echo Jesus in Matthew: "But the very hairs of your head are all numbered." The second question asks what you need to know to live and die in this comfort, and answers in three parts: how great my sin and misery are, how I am set free from them, and how I am to thank God for that freedom. Guilt, grace and gratitude, as some teachers put it, and the rest of the catechism follows that order. Other churches have their own catechisms; Luther wrote a small one too, back on day eight hundred fifty-eight. Heidelberg chose to begin with comfort.
screen: `WHETHER WE LIVE OR DIE, THE LORD'S.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself honestly: what is my comfort, in life and in death? Don't hurry to a right answer; notice what comes up first, a person, a place, a habit, a hope, a blank, and let it be. If you pray, set the catechism's line, I am not my own, beside whatever came up and see how they sit together; if not, stay with the question.
Only comfort. The Heidelberg Catechism's first question, and its answer: I am not my own, but belong to my faithful Savior, in life and in death.
Your line: my only comfort. Belonging, not a mood. That's day one thousand one hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: In Reformed churches that use the Heidelberg Catechism, it is taught to young people and new members, and some congregations preach through it in sections called Lord's Days over the course of a year.

notes: The opening question is given in the hook without quotation marks: the English is a paraphrase (source marked quoted: null), not any particular translation.
The date in the index hook (1563) is not stated under the claims rule; the file's hook line drops it.
'Written for the Reformed churches of a German territory called the Palatinate' and 'taught in Reformed churches to this day': standard history; confirm wording.

Q1 answer paraphrased (belonging body and soul; paid for sins; set free; not a hair falls without the Father's will; Spirit makes me willing and ready to live for him). Q2's three parts (misery, deliverance, gratitude) and the catechism's three-part structure; confirm.
'Guilt, grace and gratitude, as some teachers put it' is attributed as a teaching summary.
'Luther wrote a small one too' refers to the Small Catechism; no ranking intended.
